planting.note: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis, fence, or wall; this old Early Large-Flowered type blooms mainly on old wood, so limit hard cutting back to just after the main flush.

directions: Standishii was collected near Yedo (old Tokyo), Japan, and sent to the English nursery firm of Standish and Noble around the same period as the related cultivar 'Fortunei,' bearing lilac-purple, large-flowered blooms typical of the Early Large-Flowered Group. Charles Noble used it extensively as a breeding parent, crossing it with 'Fortunei' and various forms of Clematis patens during the Victorian clematis-breeding boom that produced many of today's popular large-flowered hybrids. It remains in cultivation today as a named historic cultivar among collectors, rather than a commonly offered retail plant. Keep the root zone cool and shaded with mulch or a low groundcover while the vine itself climbs into sun, and avoid heavy pruning since much of the display comes from the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted vines in early spring on a well-drained, sunny slope with good air circulation; this vinifera-type grape lacks the cold hardiness of American hybrid grapes.

directions: Muscat Hamburg is a classic old European wine and table grape prized for its large, oval, black-skinned berries carrying an intense, unmistakable muscat aroma and flavor. It was historically a favorite for hothouse grape culture in England and continues to be grown today both for fresh eating and as a breeding parent behind many muscat-flavored hybrid grapes developed around the world. Like other vinifera grapes it needs a long, warm growing season and lean, well-drained soil to ripen fully and resist rot, and it lacks the winter hardiness of American or French-American hybrid cultivars. Train onto a sturdy trellis and prune hard each winter, leaving only a modest number of fruiting buds to concentrate flavor in the ripening clusters.
sources: UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology

common_name: Folle Blanche Grape (Gros Plant, Historic Cognac Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted vines in early spring on a well-drained, sunny slope; this historically important French white grape is vigorous but susceptible to downy mildew in humid climates.

directions: Folle Blanche was once the principal grape of Cognac and Armagnac distillation in southwestern France, prized for thin-skinned, high-acid, high-yielding berries that made excellent base wine for brandy. Phylloxera and persistent downy mildew problems drove most growers to replace it with the hardier Ugni Blanc during the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, though it survives today in small plantings and under the local synonym Gros Plant in the Nantes region, where it still produces a lean, crisp white wine. It is a vigorous vine that ripens early to midseason but needs careful canopy management and fungicide attention in humid climates to control its susceptibility to mildew. Train onto a sturdy trellis in a well-drained, sunny site with good air movement to reduce disease pressure.
sources: UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a well-drained slope with good air circulation; this interspecific hybrid is hardier than pure vinifera types but still benefits from a sheltered site.

directions: Schuyler is a blue-black interspecific hybrid grape bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva, released in the mid-twentieth century for use in wine and juice production. It combines moderate cold hardiness from its American parentage with better fruit quality than purely native grape species, making it a useful mid-season option for growers outside the mildest vinifera-friendly climates. Like other Geneva-bred hybrids it has gone on to serve as breeding stock for further grape cultivars developed at the same research station. Train it onto a sturdy trellis and prune hard each winter to balance crop load against vine vigor.
sources: Cornell University New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Geneva)
